I'm revisiting the dream of formalizing Burnside's theorem to see if I have better luck the second time around. The first attempt included some aspirational complex character theory which would be great to have but isn't strictly required to get across the finish line. The challenge with characters is that we don't have any notion of "the set of simple distinct characters of a finite group G".

One alternative that I see as a possibility would be to state everything in terms of the JH factors of the group ring for the regular representation. The advantages would be we automatically get a finite set of simple modules which we can sum over, and it shouldn't be too hard to prove that the trace of left multiplication by any non-identity element in the regular representation is zero. The downside is that when we then rearrange that sum to state that for g \ne e, 0 = 1 + \sum_{m non-trivial quotient module of kG} restriction of left-multiplication action of g to m? That sum gets fuzzy there because I'm sure where we're going. Are we creating a definition of what it means for the action to be nontrivial and then using that as a clause? It feels like we avoided the trouble with asserting that we had a finite set of representatives of the isomorphism classes of our representations, only to get into swampy territory later on when replace our character sum with a sum of a different type of objects: quotient modules of the group ring.

If I stayed with the textbook version of the proof we would have a second choice between declaring "there exists a Finset of elements of Representation k G such that \forall i \ne j S i \ne S j, and \forall \rho : Representation k G \exists i such that S i = \rho" which is easy to work with but kicks the can down the road, or somehow getting into the category theory of the skeleton category of simple objects in Rep k G. Option a) is taking out a sorry I don't really know how to fill, and option b) is leaving the standard categories in Mathlib and I don't know how to formalize the process of saying "treat these representatives as a (finite!) set of members of the original category".

Between options 1, 2a, and 2b which seems like a better path and why? What is easy on a whiteboard is not always the easy way here it seems. All three options seem like they have a something really difficult, it's just a different problem with each of the routes.
Can you use class functions, with the condition that there exists some irrep of which they are the trace?
@Ryan Smith, have you seen UnitaryDual in YaelDillies/mean-fourier ?
I am proving Peter-Weyl for compact groups in the coming few weeks
I understand building on top of a moving library is a bit scary, but it would help me a lot if you did buil on top of mean-fourier, as it would give me insight on what's usable and what's not

@Scott Carnahan Are you suggesting to view characters as elements of the vector space of k valued functions on the set of conjugacy classes of G, which just happen to have a connection with a representation? Or as a subset of the vector space defined by the existence of a representation whose trace is equal on every conjugacy class? We certainly could express our characters as a particular set of class functions which happily enough forms a basis for the set of class functions.

So I think I see the outline of what you might mean, but can you be a little more specific about how we would do this?

I am suggesting that they are functions on the set of conjugacy classes (or perhaps conjugation-invariant functions on the group - I don’t know which is better). Inside this space of functions, the characters of actual representations form an integral fan.
